title: Symphony No. 7 in C major, “Leningrad”
hook: Begun in Leningrad as the siege closed in, and played there by a starving orchestra in August 1942.

painting.title: View of the Peter and Paul Fortress and the Palace Embankment
painting.pairingNote: St Petersburg in peacetime, the city Shostakovich was born in and dedicated this symphony to, painted almost a century and a half before the siege.

facts: Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941. Shostakovich was in Leningrad, his home city, and wrote the first three movements there over the summer and early autumn, as German armies surrounded the city and the bombing began. In September he spoke on Leningrad radio, telling listeners he had just finished two movements of a new symphony. In October he was evacuated, and he finished the work in Kuybyshev (today Samara) in December 1941.

The first performance was in Kuybyshev on 5 March 1942, under Samuil Samosud. The score was copied onto microfilm and taken via Tehran to the West; Arturo Toscanini conducted it on American radio on 19 July 1942. Within months it was a symbol of resistance across the Allied world.

In besieged Leningrad it was played on 9 August 1942. The Radio Orchestra under Karl Eliasberg had shrunk to about fifteen players; the rest were found around the city or sent from army bands, and the musicians got extra food. The concert was broadcast by radio and loudspeakers, and Soviet guns shelled the German positions beforehand to keep them quiet. A story often told says the date was the one Hitler had chosen to celebrate the city’s fall with a banquet at the Astoria Hotel.

What the symphony is about has been argued ever since. Officially it was the war against fascism. Some of Shostakovich’s friends later said the famous march had been sketched before the invasion, and the memoir *Testimony*, published by Solomon Volkov in 1979 and disputed ever since, has him say the symphony is also about the Leningrad that Stalin had destroyed. He gave the movements titles, “War”, “Reminiscences”, “Home Expanses” and “Victory”, and then withdrew them.
bigPicture.inOneLine: peace, then an invasion (I), a gentle memory (II), a lament for the homeland (III), a long climb to victory (IV).

movements.heading: Allegretto
movements.summary: The longest movement, and the most famous. Two calm themes paint a world at peace. Then a snare drum starts tapping far away, and a trivial little march tune is repeated, louder and louder, until it crushes everything. What follows the march is the part Shostakovich himself called the heart of the movement: a requiem.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a broad, striding melody in the strings, all playing together.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a gentle violin song over a soft, swaying accompaniment.

mainIdeas.name: The march, known as the “invasion” theme
mainIdeas.description: a jaunty, simple tune over a snare-drum rhythm that never changes. Its second half echoes a song from Lehár’s operetta *The Merry Widow*.

stops.hear: The strings together, strong and confident, in a broad, striding melody; the woodwinds answer
stops.happening: Theme 1, in [[unison|unison]]. Open-air, optimistic music

stops.hear: Quieter violins sing a long, gentle melody over a soft, rocking accompaniment
stops.happening: Theme 2. A picture of peace

stops.hear: A piccolo, then a solo violin, very high and soft; the music almost stops
stops.happening: The end of the [[exposition|exposition]]. The calm before the march

stops.hear: A snare drum, barely audible, taps a rhythm; the strings play a jaunty little tune very softly
stops.happening: The “invasion” episode begins: a 22-bar tune over a snare-drum [[ostinato|ostinato]]

stops.hear: The same tune again and again: a flute, then a piccolo, then oboe and bassoon, each time a little louder
stops.happening: Each repeat is a [[variation|variation]] in colour only; Shostakovich expected comparisons with Ravel’s *Boléro*

stops.hear: The brass take the tune, then the whole orchestra; the little march has become a brutal stamp
stops.happening: The [[crescendo|crescendo]] reaches full force. The tune is heard twelve times in all

stops.hear: Over the drum, the brass hurl out a new, falling theme, and the music reels
stops.happening: The march is answered, and the episode reaches its climax

stops.hear: The drum stops; the orchestra cries out the opening theme, now harsh and anguished
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]] begins, with Theme 1 in distress

stops.hear: A solo bassoon, almost alone, sings a long, grieving melody
stops.happening: The requiem. Shostakovich said this, not the march, was the centre of the movement

stops.hear: The opening theme returns softly in the strings
stops.happening: Theme 1, gentle and tired

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: A muted trumpet recalls the march tune; the snare drum taps far away
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]. The march has not gone away

notice: Listen to the snare drum in the invasion episode. It plays the same rhythm for more than ten minutes without a break, while everything above it grows.

Shostakovich said he did not want to depict battle, with planes and tanks; he wanted to convey “the context of grim events”. The march is not frightening at first. It becomes frightening by being repeated.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Vasily Petrenko was born in Leningrad in 1976. He recorded the symphony in Liverpool in June 2012, as part of his complete cycle of Shostakovich’s symphonies for Naxos. His first movement is broad, almost half an hour long.

movements.heading: Moderato (poco allegretto)
movements.summary: A quiet, melancholy [[scherzo|scherzo]], the shortest movement. Shostakovich described it as happy memories wrapped in a gentle sadness, like a mist. A shrill middle section breaks the spell for a while.

stops.hear: The violins, softly, in a light, delicate tune
stops.happening: The scherzo begins in a whisper

stops.hear: A solo oboe, high and wistful, plays a long melody over the strings
stops.happening: The movement’s sad, singing heart

stops.hear: A shrill, high clarinet breaks in with a harsh, jerky tune
stops.happening: The middle section ([[trio|trio]])

stops.hear: Brass and full orchestra, loud and driving, over a hammering rhythm
stops.happening: The trio’s climax, built on another [[ostinato|ostinato]]

stops.hear: Quiet again: the light opening tune returns
stops.happening: The scherzo comes back

stops.hear: The oboe’s melody, now lower and darker in another woodwind
stops.happening: The memory returns, greyer than before

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The sound thins out and fades
stops.happening: A soft ending

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: The emotional centre of the symphony, first called “Home Expanses”. Solemn wind chords alternate with a long, speaking melody in the violins. A fierce, fast middle section interrupts, and then the solemn music returns and leads straight into the finale.

stops.hear: Woodwinds and horns, loud and slow, in solemn chords
stops.happening: A [[chorale|chorale]]: grand and grieving at once

stops.hear: The violins, all together, in a long, declaiming melody
stops.happening: A melody like a speech, close to [[recitative|recitative]]

stops.hear: The wind chords return; the strings answer
stops.happening: The two ideas take turns

stops.hear: A solo flute sings a long, gentle tune over soft plucked strings
stops.happening: A pastoral memory, the calmest music in the symphony

stops.hear: The pace quickens; the low strings drive a repeated figure; the brass rise up
stops.happening: The fast middle section

stops.hear: The whole orchestra at full force
stops.happening: The climax of the movement

stops.hear: The wind chorale returns, then the violins’ speaking melody
stops.happening: The opening music comes back

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Very quiet; the music runs straight on into the finale
stops.happening: No pause

notice: Compare the flute’s solo at ≈ 5:00 with the bassoon’s requiem in the first movement. Shostakovich gives the most personal music in this huge orchestra to single wind players.

movements.heading: Allegro non troppo
movements.summary: The finale begins in near silence and has to fight its way to victory. A fast, driving struggle, a slow and heavy lament, and then one long, steady build to the end, where the very first theme of the symphony returns in a blaze of C major.

stops.hear: Very quiet strings and a soft drum roll, as if from far away
stops.happening: The finale grows out of the Adagio without a break

stops.hear: A short rhythm, three quick notes and a long one, softly in the strings
stops.happening: A rhythm that runs through the finale. Some writers hear Morse code “V”, for victory

stops.hear: The low strings start a quick, march-like tune; the violins and the orchestra answer
stops.happening: The struggle begins

stops.hear: High strings in quick three-note figures; cellos and basses snap their strings against the fingerboard
stops.happening: A tense, rattling passage, with hard [[pizzicato|pizzicato]]

stops.hear: Slow, heavy, accented music, like a solemn dance
stops.happening: A mourning section in the manner of a [[sarabande|sarabande]]

stops.hear: Quiet again; a long, steady climb begins
stops.happening: The final crescendo starts

stops.hear: The brass blaze out the opening theme of the first movement, now in C major
stops.happening: The goal of the whole symphony

stops.label: Last bars
stops.hear: The full orchestra and drums hammer out the final chords
stops.happening: The end, in C major

notice: The tune at ≈ 17:00 is Theme 1 from the very start of the symphony. Eighty minutes later it returns, and the question is whether it sounds like the same music.

threads.title: Marches and machines
threads.body: The invasion march in the first movement, the hammering middle of the second, the driving figures in the Adagio and the finale: repeated rhythms keep taking over.

threads.title: Single voices
threads.body: In between the masses of sound, single players carry the grief: the bassoon’s requiem, the oboe in the scherzo, the flute in the Adagio.

threads.title: A symbol and a puzzle
threads.body: In 1942 the symphony was a public weapon, played in a starving city and broadcast to the world. What Shostakovich meant by it in private is still debated.
